summary:
Allwork.Space argues that most organizations lack "spatial intelligence": they know square footage, cost per square foot, energy costs and occupancy rates, but not how the office is actually used. A Wakefield Research survey of 400 workplace decision makers found 62% cannot determine space usage without asking employees directly or deploying privacy-compromising monitoring technology, neither of which produces genuine insight (surveys yield what leadership wants to hear; monitoring erodes trust and drives performative behavior).

Consequences cited: 36% rely on gut instinct for decisions about amenities, redesign and lease size; 76% worry their layout is not delivering productive use of space; 24% of under- or unoccupied space is regularly heated and cooled. These costs land as productivity loss, retention issues, energy spend and capital expense, at a moment when fit-out investment is rising. JLL reports 59% of organizations are increasing office fit-out investment, with renovation costs up 2% to 6% globally and North America highest at $230 to $375 per square foot.

The common remedy, stitching together occupancy counters, badge swipes and room reservation systems into a dashboard, leaves a blind spot: it captures who is in the building and for how long, not how behavior shifts through the day or season. Examples include sun glare pushing people to relocate or leave. Survey respondents see savings potential in energy (62%) and cleaning (60%).

The piece promotes thermal sensing as an anonymous alternative, since it reads body heat rather than capturing images. Mapped to floorplans, thermal data revealed one employer lacked conference rooms and private work areas; another saves $1,400 per restroom per year. AI is positioned as the layer that turns millions of frames into trend narratives and recommendations on layout, desk assignments and scheduling models, including modeling spikes in support desk calls. Conclusion: office investment decisions should be rooted in real, anonymized behavioral data.

claims.attribution: Wakefield Research survey of 400 workplace decision makers
